chapter_theme: The war of the plough-bearer against the Vidyadhara brothers: the young hero is attacked by four, the plough and lion bring his side back, Ratna Greevan's mountain breaks the army until an arrow fells him, and the grieving Asvagriva looses a spell that calls Death and the spirits against the world.

cast.role: the white plough-bearing hero, called வெள்ளியான் and அலாயுதன்; read as Vijayan
the younger brothers of Asvagriva (Kireevan) who attack the young hero
one of the attackers, with Vayira Kandan
the warrior who lifts the mountain
called also கனக நாமன், who fights the plough-bearer
the archer who looses the sun-bright arrow
those who report the deaths to Asvagriva
the lord of the gold discus, the Vidyadha king, who sends the spell
the spell that Asvagriva sends out
the spirits and ghoul-hosts that gather

1407.reading: Headless trunks dance with ringing anklets on the field, and the clotted flesh lit with fire looks like lamps set on stumps.

1408.reading: The white hero ploughs the field of battle with his plough, using the Vidyadharas' blood as water, and sows his fame in it.
1408.nuance: The plough-warrior is not named by a proper name here; the plough (நாஞ்சில்) and the epithet 'the white one' point to Vijayan, and 1418 names the same fighter அலாயுதன், the plough-bearer.
1408.event: The white hero ploughs the battlefield with his plough and sows fame in the Vidyadhara blood.

1409.reading: The younger brothers of Kireevan, hearing of a merciless youth who has taken the field, ask who he is.
1409.nuance: Lines 1-2 give the youth's red eyes and the field he now holds in broken word division; only the question in the closing lines is firm.
1409.event: Greevan's younger brothers ask who the youth is that has taken over the battle.

1410.reading: Resenting that this one is the eldest of the Suramai lord's sons, four young warriors drive their elephants at him alone.
1410.nuance: Who the four are and who the one is cannot be fixed from the verse; I read the four as the younger Vidyadhara champions of 1409 and the one as the young hero the Suramai lord's son.
1410.event: Four young warriors, burning with anger, drive elephants against one man.

1411.reading: Ratna Kandan and the other warriors block the lanes of the oncoming force, burn them, and close on the young hero in fury.
1411.event: Ratna Kandan and three others cut off and attack the young hero.

1412.reading: A cry goes up that the young prince has fallen, and the Suramai king's army heaves like a dark sea over a whirlpool.
1412.nuance: The cry may be a rumour; 1413 and 1414 show the young prince's side recovering at once, so the fall is not shown as final.
1412.event: The army of the Suramai king is thrown into confusion by the cry that the young prince has fallen.

1413.reading: A lion-like hero, new in the fight, mounts a fierce lion and takes up a new plough.
1413.nuance: Line 1-2 are obscure and the rider is not named; the plough makes Vijayan the likely reader.
1413.event: The hero mounts a lion and takes a fresh plough.

1414.reading: The plough, the red-eyed lion and the elder brother arrive and the young king's army roars, while the enemy's elephants break in confusion.
1414.nuance: 'The young king' here is the younger of the two brothers, which is why 1412's cry is answered now.
1414.event: The elder brother arrives with plough and lion; the young king's army roars and the enemy's elephants scatter.

1415.reading: In the thick of the fight he ploughs open the broad rich chests of the proud warriors, the youth who can bewilder even the best of them.
1415.event: The young hero ploughs open the enemy warriors' chests with his plough.

1416.reading: Kanaka Naman, hearing that one man with a plough has beaten two men and four elephants, comes to the fight, shoulders like a dark mountain.
1416.event: Kanaka Naman, hearing of the plough-bearer's feats, joins the battle.

1417.reading: Kanaka Chitran, angry, wipes his sword's edge and strikes, and the lion-like plough-bearer drives the plough's tip into his shoulder.
1417.nuance: Chapter 60 casts Kanaka Chitran as a son of the discus-holder who steps in for the kings; here he fights the plough-bearer, so the two scenes are not shown to be on one side.
1417.event: Kanaka Chitran strikes with his sword and the plough-bearer pins his shoulder with the plough's blade.

1418.reading: Hearing that Vayira Kandan and all the others were beaten by Alaayudhan and what became of Kanaka Chitran, one man is left with a heart on fire.
1418.nuance: The man who burns is not named; 1419 names Ratna Greevan as the next to act, so I read him.
1418.event: A warrior, learning of the defeat of Vayira Kandan and the rest, is left burning with anger.

1419.reading: Ratna Greevan rises in rage, resolved to finish the fight and manhood of those of the earth, and lifts a great mountain in his diamond-hard hands.
1419.event: Ratna Greevan lifts a mountain with his hands.

1420.reading: Belted, bearded and with brows knit, he blazes like fire and lifts the mountain and advances, and the army of the Suramai king scatters.
1420.event: The army of the Suramai king scatters as Ratna Greevan advances with the mountain.

1421.reading: As he comes close, an arrow gleams in the quiver of the king and into Arukka Kirti's drawn bow, and he sets it and drives it on.
1421.nuance: Line 1-2 turn on a rare construction 'அருக்க கீர்த்தி கை'; the archer is read as Arukka Kirti.
1421.event: Arukka Kirti fits a bright arrow to his bow and shoots.

1422.reading: The arrow he strung, shot, set to the shoulder, tore through and drove into the earth, and it laid low even the onlookers: they call it the sun's arrow.
1422.event: The arrow pierces its target, enters the earth and strikes down bystanders.

1423.reading: The garlanded hero falls like one mountain on another and the sea churns while the hills grieve.
1423.nuance: The faller is not named; it follows the arrow of 1421-1422 and the mountain-lifter of 1419-1420, so I read Ratna Greevan.
1423.event: A great hero falls like a mountain and the sea and hills tremble.

1424.reading: The staff-bearing messengers run to the lord of the gold discus and tell him that his younger brothers' sons and heroes died, the words falling on his ear like molten copper.
1424.nuance: The words in line 4 'அரக்குண் கோலோர்' are rare; I read them as the staff-bearers of 055's report, not fixed.
1424.event: Messengers report the deaths of his kinsmen and heroes to the discus-holding king.

1425.reading: Dark as a mountain, he asks what is left to him if these are the news and chooses to loose the spell that sweeps up all living things of the world and pours them into the sea.
1425.nuance: Grief and rage give the decision, and the verse states no claim on its justice; the Jain epic lets the reader see the sweep of the spell as the work of anger.
1425.event: Asvagriva decides to send out a spell that gathers all life into the sea.

1426.reading: At the thought the spell stands close, Chandavegai, and he bids it take every human of the sea-bound world, if it can, choosing them out and sparing none.
1426.nuance: 'Choosing out and leaving none' (line 3-4) is odd: it can bid the spell to seek each person out, or to take them all without distinction; either way no sparing is allowed.
1426.event: Asvagriva commands the spell Chandavegai to destroy mankind.

1427.reading: When he sends the spell, it calls Death, laughs showing sharp teeth, tells him the world will end in its mouth at the sun-bright king's wish, and bids Death finish his own task too.
1427.event: The spell Chandavegai summons Death and tells him to do his task as the world is ended.

1428.reading: The spirits gather and say they will fill their great bellies too, dance with bright tridents and bow round, and the great goddess comes and drives the spell on the Suramai king's army.
1428.event: The spirits and the great goddess come and the spell is loosed upon the Suramai king's army.

1429.reading: The ghoul-hosts come crying, long-footed, hollow-bellied, with hair-covered fingers and rolling round eyes like gall-nuts.

1430.reading: The spell shows as wind that rolls mountains, a fire that rises in rows, and a deep sea thrown up, as the god of rich colour sends it forth.
1430.nuance: The scope of the destruction is as great as that of the end of an age, yet the target is one army; the epic holds both.
1430.event: The spell appears as storm-wind, fire and sea.

1431.reading: The wind and fire shaking down mountains, trees and earth join, and the sea rolls over the world as if the god were devouring it.
1431.nuance: Line 4 begins with a broken word 'கிள ருலகை' and the last sentence is held loosely.
1431.event: Wind, fire and sea together destroy mountains, trees and earth.

links.note: 1408 sows fame in a field ploughed with the plough; 1415 ploughs open the warriors' chests with the same plough.
links.teaches: The metaphor of a farmer's field opens as a boast and returns as the literal wound, showing the plough as both sign and tool of the hero's rule over the battle.

links.note: 1412 cries that the young prince has fallen and the army heaves; 1414 brings the elder brother and the plough and the army roars again.
links.teaches: The army's despair and its roar are made by one man's presence, so the verses show whom its courage hangs on.

links.note: 1416 shows Kanaka Naman coming to the fight on hearing of the plough-bearer; 1417 shows him struck on the shoulder.
links.teaches: The listener who joins a fight because he heard of a rival's feats is also the one who is struck down, so the fame that draws him is what ruins him.

links.note: 1418 leaves one man burning at the news of defeat; 1419 has Ratna Greevan lift the mountain.
links.teaches: The news of the defeat is turned into an act, which shows what anger does with grief in the epic's warriors.

links.note: 1419 lifts the mountain; 1420 shows the Suramai army scattering as he advances.
links.teaches: The scattering shows that the mountain wins by fear before it falls, so the plough-bearer's earlier victory is reversed here.

links.note: 1424 brings the messengers' report; 1425 has the king resolve to loose the spell.
links.teaches: The report is the whole cause of the spell, so the epic ties the world's destruction to one man's grief.

links.note: 1426 orders the spell to destroy mankind; 1427 has the spell pass the work on to Death.
links.teaches: The command goes from king to spell to Death, so the epic shows destruction as a chain of obedience with no one pausing.

links.note: 1427 has the spell call Death; 1428 shows the spirits and the goddess coming and the spell loosed on the army.
links.teaches: Death's summons is joined by a feast of spirits, which shows the destruction as a gathering that feeds many.

links.note: 1420 shows an army scattering before a mountain-lifter; Kural 765 sets the standard of an army that stands together even when Death comes at it.
links.teaches: The scene gives the Kural's test a failure that the couplet only describes as a standard, and shows the Kural's army needs a leader to hold.

gains.a: the unit gains a measure by which the scattering is a failure of the army and not only the fault of one man
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene where the standard is not met, showing what its unbroken army is set against

links.note: 1425 has a king's grief and anger lead him to loose a spell that destroys the world; Kural 305 says anger kills the one who does not guard against it.
links.teaches: The epic shows anger as a power that reaches the world and not only the angry man, which limits the couplet's 'yourself'.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule that makes the king's anger the cause of what follows and not only an act of war
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the harm of anger goes outward and the self is not the only victim

links.note: 1426 has a king order the destruction of all men; Tirumanthiram 238 says an unlearned king who says 'kill' is worse than Death, since Death spares the good.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the king who commands total death is judged by a rule the epic's own narrator does not state.

gains.a: the unit gains a standard by which its royal order is judged as the act of a king who says 'kill'
gains.b: the verse gains a case of a king with the power to turn Death into his tool

links.note: 1427 has a spell command Death to finish his work at a king's wish; Tirumanthiram 176 says no one can fight when life leaves and only the thought of the Lord turns Death's messengers.
links.teaches: The epic's Death takes orders from a spell while the Saiva verse holds Death answerable to the Lord alone, so the two disagree over who commands Death.

gains.a: the unit gains a view in which Death does not serve a king's spell
gains.b: the verse gains a scene where Death is commanded by a human wish, which the verse denies

source_issues: Verses 1425-1431 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 lines by the repair tool.
Verse 1431 line 4 has a broken word division ('கிள ருலகை') and 1407 has an odd form 'பாய்ந்தழெக்'.
Who fights whom in 1409-1411 and who falls in 1423 cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone.
